analysis.one_liner: Restores court review (habeas corpus) for detainees, undoing the Military Commissions Act's limits.
analysis.headline: The bill was sent to three House committees, referred to a subcommittee in March 2007, and never received a vote before the 110th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2006, Congress passed the Military Commissions Act, which limited the ability of people held in U.S. custody — including non-citizens living in the United States — to ask a federal court to review their detention, a protection known as habeas corpus. This bill said that nothing in that Act could take away the right of any U.S. resident to habeas corpus, and that the right should be read under the Constitution's due process protections. The bill was introduced with a mix of Democratic and Republican support but was never taken up by any committee and died when the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone held by the U.S. government as a terrorism suspect, including non-citizen residents of the United States, would regain the ability to challenge their detention in federal court rather than being held indefinitely with no judicial review. More broadly, all U.S. residents benefit from keeping a constitutional check on executive detention power.

how_it_helps.text: The bill provides that nothing in the Military Commissions Act of 2006 or its amendments shall affect the right of any U.S. resident to habeas corpus, restoring access to federal courts to challenge detention.
It directs that this right be construed in accordance with the 5th and 14th Amendments, grounding the protection in the Constitution's due process guarantees.

analysis.who_pays: The executive branch would lose the ability to hold detainees outside the reach of federal courts, and terrorism cases would face court challenges that the government argues complicate national security operations. Taxpayer costs are minor; the main cost is to government flexibility in detention policy.

drawbacks.text: Supporters of the Military Commissions Act argued that habeas petitions from terrorism suspects could burden the courts and interfere with wartime detention and intelligence operations, by giving captured fighters a way to litigate their captivity.
The bill addresses only the Military Commissions Act of 2006 by name, so a future statute could still attempt to limit habeas corpus unless Congress acted again.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is the restoration of a core constitutional protection — the right to have a neutral court review whether the government is holding someone lawfully — for anyone detained on U.S. soil. The cost is real but narrow: the executive branch loses a tool for holding suspects outside judicial oversight, and some detention decisions would face litigation. On balance the protection outweighs the inconvenience to government operations, which is the standard trade Congress has made for two centuries of habeas practice.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three committees at once and then to a Judiciary subcommittee, and no committee ever brought it up for a vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. David Wu introduced the bill on February 16, 2007, joined by six original cosponsors from both parties.
The House referred it simultaneously to the Armed Services, Judiciary, and Foreign Affairs Committees, a split that placed it before multiple committees with no requirement that any of them act.
In March 2007 it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties, where it remained without a hearing or markup.
The bill drew 8 cosponsors, 4 Republicans and 4 Democrats, but received no further action and died when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The executive branch kept the detention powers created by the Military Commissions Act of 2006, and detainees at Guantanamo and elsewhere remained without the habeas review this bill would have restored. No member ever had to cast a recorded vote on the issue.

for.name: Rep. David Wu
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Habeas Corpus Preservation Act on February 16, 2007.

for.name: 4 of 202 House Republicans
for.role: Original cosponsors (Reps. Jones of NC, LaTourette, Gilchrest, Bartlett)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, giving it bipartisan support from the start.

for.name: 4 of 233 House Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors (Reps. Larson, DeFazio, and two others)

against.name: Rep. John Conyers Jr.
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee of primary jurisdiction after the bill was sent to its Constitution subcommittee; the committee never reported the bill or held a vote on it.

against.name: House Armed Services and Foreign Affairs Committees
against.role: Co-referred committees, chaired by Democrats in the 110th Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action on it during the Congress.

against.name: George W. Bush administration
against.what_they_did: Opposed restoring habeas corpus rights stripped by the Military Commissions Act of 2006, whose detention and trial framework the bill would have undone.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from introduction — of the bill's 8 cosponsors, 4 were Republicans and 4 were Democrats — and the record shows no vote at which party lines could form; the bill died in committee.

industries.industry: Executive detention and military-commission authority (federal government)
industries.note: The bill would have stripped the executive's power to hold detainees without federal court review, a power created by the Military Commissions Act of 2006. Unreviewed detention authority runs against the public's interest in judicial oversight of government power.
